headline: Ancient Canadian fossils push back the origins of animal life
meta_description: A remarkable fossil site in Canada's Northwest Territories reveals that complex animal life emerged 5–10 million years earlier than scientists previously thoug…
summary_short: Scientists in Canada's Northwest Territories discovered 567-million-year-old fossils that rewrite when animals first moved and reproduced sexually.
body:
A remote fossil site in Canada's Mackenzie Mountains is reshaping our understanding of when complex animal life first emerged. Researchers have uncovered more than 100 specimens dating back 567 million years, pushing back key evolutionary milestones by 5 to 10 million years. The discovery reveals that animals were already moving, reproducing sexually, and developing recognizable body plans far earlier than previous evidence suggested. Scott Evans, the study's lead author at the American Museum of Natural History, describes the significance: for three billion years, life on Earth was dominated by microbes—then suddenly, large, complex animals appeared capable of behaviors we recognize today. This new site offers crucial insight into that mysterious transition.

The fossils belong to the Ediacaran biota, a collection of soft-bodied organisms that lived on ancient seafloors more than 500 million years ago. Before this discovery, White Sea fossils—one of three major groups of Ediacaran organisms—had been documented only in Europe, Asia, and Australia. The Canadian site is notable for containing six groups never previously recorded in North America. Among the newly found creatures is Dickinsonia, a flat animal that absorbed nutrients through its lower surface, and Funisia, a tube-shaped organism that provides the oldest known evidence of sexual reproduction through coordinated release of sperm and eggs into water.

The fossil-bearing layers are covered by hundreds of feet of rock that may contain many more specimens, suggesting vast potential for future discoveries. The work was conducted on traditional lands of the Sahtú Dene and Métis communities, whose members guided and permitted the research. Scientists emphasize that this site fills a critical gap in our geological record of early animal life, offering new opportunities to understand how and where complex life first flourished on our planet.
quick_facts: 567-million-year-old fossils found in Canada's Mackenzie Mountains
Discovery pushes back animal evolution by 5–10 million years
More than 100 specimens including six groups never before found in North America
Site contains oldest known evidence of sexual reproduction in animals
Research conducted on Sahtú Dene and Métis traditional lands
